Newly hatched paralarvae of the Fourhorn octopus emerge with a mantle length of just 0.45 cm [Lb = 0.45 cm], a diminutive size that reflects the substantial energetic investment in yolk reserves during embryonic development. Field observations suggest that these minute individuals drift as planktonic organisms for an extended period, relying on small crustaceans as their initial prey following the onset of exogenous feeding. The early life stages of Pteroctopus tetracirrhus are notably vulnerable to predation, and the small body size at hatching likely necessitates a high growth rate to reduce mortality risk during the first weeks of benthic settlement.

Upon reaching sexual maturation, females of this species attain a mantle length at puberty of 10.5 cm [Lp = 10.5 cm], while males become reproductively competent at a somewhat smaller size, with a mantle length at puberty of 8.5 cm [Lp = 8.5 cm] recorded in laboratory-reared individuals. This size dimorphism at the onset of gonadal activity is consistent with patterns observed in other benthic octopus species, where differential reproductive strategies between sexes drive variation in body size trajectories. The onset of gametogenesis appears tightly coupled with the acquisition of a threshold body size, after which individuals shift their energetic priorities towards reproduction.

The total fecundity of this species is considerable, with a single female capable of producing approximately 8000 eggs  during a single spawning event when maintained at a stable water temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. This high egg count is characteristic of many octopus species that exhibit terminal reproduction, where females invest the entirety of their remaining somatic reserves into a single, large clutch following mating. The eggs themselves are relatively small and are typically attached in strings to the underside of rocky crevices, where the female provides continuous care until the paralarvae emerge.

Maximum longevity in female Fourhorn octopus has been estimated at 530 days [am = 530 days] under captive conditions at a constant temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], a lifespan that is comparatively short and reflects the semelparous reproductive strategy typical of many incirrate octopuses. The life cycle culminates in a single, synchronized reproductive effort, after which females cease feeding and eventually succumb to physiological exhaustion. The duration of this post-reproductive brooding period, during which the female guards her developing eggs without foraging, constitutes a significant portion of the total lifespan and imposes a severe energetic cost.

Males of Pteroctopus tetracirrhus achieve a final mantle length at death of 9.5 cm [Li = 9.5 cm] and a corresponding wet weight at death of 374.0 grams [Wwi = 374.0 grams], whereas females grow to a larger terminal size, with a mantle length at death of 11.0 cm [Li = 11.0 cm] and a wet weight at death of 741.0 grams [Wwi = 741.0 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism in favor of females is thought to be linked to the demands of egg production and brooding, where a larger body cavity accommodates greater ovarian capacity. The substantial difference in terminal body mass between the sexes underscores the divergent energetic allocations that characterize the reproductive biology of this species.
